metric.production_adoption_deployment_ev.limitations: Survey percentages and download counts are reported here as one corroborating data point among three independent rubric legs (named-company evidence, platform-native-support evidence, survey evidence), not as the sole basis for the score, per the methodology's restriction on standalone popularity proxies. Some sourced commentary pages are SEO/marketing-style aggregator content rather than primary company engineering posts; the strongest primary evidence used above is the conference-talk citation (Airbnb/Brie Bunge, JSConf Hawaii 2019) relayed through a secondary source, and Microsoft/Slack/Shopify migrations are cited via a secondary aggregator rather than each company's own blog, which is disclosed as a source-quality limitation.
metric.production_adoption_deployment_ev.selection_rule: Use public, independently checkable production evidence; named deployments must be documented by the deploying organization or corroborated by credible independent sources. Popularity surveys alone do not prove deployment.

metric.third_party_tool_availability.limitations: Weekly npm download / dependent-project counts and GitHub stars are used here only as one corroborating signal for tool reuse breadth, not as the sole basis for the score; they are combined with official-documentation citations (Microsoft's own editor-support wiki and tooling blog) and independent comparative tooling analyses, consistent with the methodology's restriction on using raw popularity counts as a standalone proxy.
metric.third_party_tool_availability.selection_rule: Inspect the same fixed tool categories for every language and require independently maintained current tools; official first-party tools may be cited only as context, not as third-party availability.
